items.title: Two ways to open a condition

states.label: With the if-word
states.sm: ʻĀfai e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.
states.en: If it rains tomorrow, the trip will not go.
states.note: The if-word opens a condition with a tense particle of its own.

states.label: With the short future particle
states.sm: ʻĀ timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.
states.en: When it rains tomorrow, the trip will not go.
states.note: The short future particle stands alone. English may use if, when or whenever for this shape, according to the situation.

items.caption: The condition comes first in both. The second shape has no separate joining word before its short future particle.

items.title: An open condition or an expected one

states.label: Open
states.sm: ʻĀfai e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.
states.en: If it rains tomorrow, the trip will not go.
states.note: The general particle leaves the condition open.

states.label: More expected
states.sm: ʻĀfai ʻoleʻā timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.
states.en: If it is going to rain tomorrow, the trip will not go.
states.note: The future particle carries a much higher degree of certainty than the general particle.

items.caption: The if-word stays in place. The tense particle inside the condition changes how expected the condition is.

items.title: Find the condition in the sentence

prompts.sm: ʻĀfai e iai se apu, ʻou te ʻai.
prompts.why: The if-word opens the first clause; the eating follows it.

prompts.sm: Sau vave pē ʻāfai ʻoleʻā maua le meaʻai.
prompts.why: The command comes first. *Pē* stands in front of the following condition.

prompts.sm: E lē alu le tama i le matafaga pē ʻā afa.
prompts.why: The main clause is followed by *pē* and the condition opened by the short future particle.

items.intro: Read which clause says what has to be true, then choose its position.
